Items.Authors: A. Brucalassi, J. A. Araiza-Durán, P. Picchi, A. Tozzi, A. G. Pérez, A. J. Fernandez-Soler, C. Galy, A. Caldwell, A. Fitzpatrick, A. Bocchieri, E. Pascale, J. Pérez Álvarez, G. Morgante, D. Bruzzi, M. E. Caldwell, V. D. Cardinale, P. Chioetto, F. D'Anca, P. Eccleston, D. Ferruzzi, D. Gottini, E. Guerriero, D. Jollet, R. Lilli, G. Micela, A. Olivieri, E. Pace, G. Preti, M. Rainer, G. Savini, A. Scippa, G. Tinetti, P. Zuppella
Items.Title: ARIEL payload STOP analysis: updated results on the in-flight operational cases for the telescope assembly
Items.Abstract: At payload level, a Structural, Thermal, and Optical Performance (STOP) analysis is carried out to evaluate how thermo-elastic effects may impact the instrument’s optical performance. A STOP analysis integrates structural, thermal, and optical models to predict how temperature variations and mechanically induced deformations propagate through the telescope assembly and ultimately affect key optical metrics such as alignment, wavefront error, and imaging quality. This coupled approach enables the estimation of performance degradation under representative environmental load cases and supports verification of compliance with scientific and engineering requirements.    This document presents the updated results of the optical design analysis performed to predict the in-flight performance for the Telescope Assembly of the ESA M4 mission Ariel according to the operational scenarios defined for Cycle C-2.

Items.Authors: Yu Ding, Chen Xu, Dongsheng Niu, Xiaojun Zhou
Items.Title: Assembly and alignment of the multiplexed survey telescope wide field corrector
Items.Abstract: The 6.5m MUltiplexed Survey Telescope(MUST) proposed by Tsinghua University adopts a multiple-element widefield corrector (WFC) to achieve large field of view. The WFC consists of five large lenses, two of which are wedge-shaped lenses and act as an atmospheric dispersion corrector. The first lens element has a diameter of 1. 6 meters, while the diameters of the remaining elements range from 1.36 to 1.45 meters. To meet the excellent image quality, each lens was aligned to be well within 20μm and 9arcsec, which is a major challenge. This will be achieved by using a centration measurement instrument supplemented by contact metrology methods. The centration measurement instrument is based on self-collimating imaging principle, with a maximum test diameter of 2m and an accuracy of 2μm. This paper details the design of the large centration measurement instrument, outlines the alignment and assembly procedures and presents the latest results.

Items.Authors: Aashia Rahman, Anna M. Weiß, Carlos Enrique Rodriguez Alvarez, Ria G. Krämer, Kalaga Madhav, Xijie Luo, Stefan Nolte
Items.Title: Athermal package for OH-emission filters for ground-based astronomy: part III: stability assessment
Items.Abstract: Fiber Bragg gratings (FBGs) are promising hydroxyl (OH) line filters for ground-based NIR astronomy, but effective suppression requires thermal stability within the tolerance set by the resolving power (R) of the spectrograph used. We analyzed the stability of 20 FBG notches matched to OH lines between 1540 nm and 1590 nm, arranged in five arrays. Four arrays were conventionally mounted on aluminum plates without temperature compensation, while one was housed in an in-house-manufactured athermal package. Using a broadband source and an optical spectrum analyzer (R ≈ 77,500), we assessed short-term and long-term stability across 24°C to 29°C. The athermalized array showed significantly improved wavelength stability compared with the conventional mounts, underscoring the importance of thermal compensation. Accelerated temperature cycling (25°C to 30°C, 3 cycles/2 h) using an in-house astrophotonic spectrograph (R ≈ 10,000) further demonstrated negligible drift. On-sky tests will follow.

Items.Authors: Marco Barbera, Ugo Lo Cicero, Michela Todaro, Federico Fiorentino, Luisa Sciortino, Caterina Tortorici, Fabio D'Anca, Edoardo Alaimo, Andrea Delfini, Christian Circi, Alessia Di Giacomo, Salvatore Varisco, Alberto Gulizzi, Claudio Saitta, Pekka T. Torma, Bahawal Haq, Pascal Mercere, Paulo Da Silva, Fabio Reale, Gabriele Cozzo, Daniele Brienza, Denise Perrone, Marco Stangalini, Paul Boerner, Bart De Pontieu, Marco Miceli
Items.Title: Atomic-oxygen irradiation of metal-coated carbon-nanotube-based filters developed for the NASA’s MUSE solar mission
Items.Abstract: The Multi-slit Solar Explorer (MUSE) will use a multi-slit spectrograph and a context imager to observe the  solar transition region and corona in the extreme ultraviolet. Metal-coated carbon-nanotube (CNT) pellicles  have been developed as optical blocking filters for the two instruments. Because MUSE will operate in low  Earth orbit, the filters must tolerate atomic oxygen (AtOx) without losing in-band throughput or out-of-band  rejection. We report results of a conservative AtOx irradiation and characterization test campaign performed  on four flight-model witness filters: 150-nm and 600-nm Al coatings and 200-nm and 600-nm Zr coatings on  dual-layer single-wall CNT pellicles.

Items.Authors: Tony D. Travouillon, Jeff Cooke, Matt Radovan, Adam Nagy-Sochcki, Victoria Zinnercker, Chris Stokes-Griffin, Adam Lilleyman, Shanti Krishnan
Items.Title: Automated fiber placement (AFP) carbon composite camera barrel prototype for the Keck wide field imager
Items.Abstract: The Keck Wide-Field Insturment is an Australian led instrument proposed for the Keck telescope to unlock its wide-field potential in the near UV part of the spectrum. Since it will be placed at the prime focus of the telescope, the instrument had to significantly be reduced in weight in order to minimise flexure. This required using new materials and methodology to build it major compnents.    New Frontier Technology designed and manufactured a thermoplastic composite conical lens barrel for the Keck Wide Field Imager, featuring near-zero axial coefficient of thermal expansion (CTE) (< 0.5ppm) and radial CTE (16.2 ppm) tuned to match aluminium mirror mounts. These precise thermal properties were achieved through laser-assisted automated fibre placement (AFP), which enables careful tuning of CTE via deliberate fibre orientation. The final demonstrator has a mass of 5.5 kg, representing an almost fourfold reduction compared with an equivalent aluminium design.

Items.Authors: Veronika Wimmer, Matteo Accardo, Camilo Avilés, Paulo Ferreira, Marcus Haug, Gerd Jakob, Tobias Müller, Rodrigo Olguin
Items.Title: Automated liquid nitrogen supply 2.0 at the European Southern Observatory
Items.Abstract: ESO operates several telescopes in the Atacama Desert in Chile, including the Paranal Astronomical Observatory (PAO) and the Extremely Large Telescope (ELT). All VLT and ELT instruments require powerful cryogenic cooling systems for pre-cooling and / or steady state operation to cool masses ranging from several kilograms to several tons.  This paper provides an overview of the fully operational automated Liquid Nitrogen Infrastructure (LIN IS) at ESO Headquarter in Germany, of the ELT LIN IS, which successfully passed the final design phase in 2025, and of the Phase A study for upgrading the PAO site's liquid nitrogen infrastructure similar as developed for ESO HQ and the ELT. The upgrade would entail installing a centralized, fully automated, open-loop LIN cooling system refilling all VLT cryogenic instruments to enhance operational efficiency and safety, minimize manual intervention, and align with concepts developed for HQ and ELT LIN IS, but adapted specifically for the VLT.

Items.Authors: Daksh Singh, Ting S. Li, Sarik Jerma, Shaojie Chen
Items.Title: Automated multi-stressor optical fiber focal ratio degradation and throughput characterization system for future massive multiplex spectroscopic survey
Items.Abstract: Future spectroscopic survey facilities such as Spec-S5 and the Wide-Field Spectroscopic Telescope (WST) are expected to use more than 25,000 optical fibers. Characterizing focal ratio degradation (FRD) and throughput across such large fiber populations is essential for spectroscopic calibration, sky subtraction, and overall instrument performance, but manual testing is prohibitively time-consuming. In this work, we present an automated multi-stressor optical fiber characterization system designed to measure FRD and throughput efficiently under controlled optical and mechanical conditions. The system enables measurements as a function of input angle, wavelength, bend radius, fiber twist, and applied load. We demonstrate the functionality of the system using individual fibers and fiber bundles, and present the resulting FRD and throughput profiles under a range of applied stress conditions.

Items.Authors: Thomas Procter, Megan Dubay, Hank Corbett, Nicholas Law, Jonathan Carney, James Dockery, Katie M. Fasbender, Shannon Fitton, Lawrence Machia, William Marshall, Donovan Schlekat, Alan Vasquez Soto, Jonah L. Aponte, Alex Bucheli, Thomas Cowart, Colin H. Grimes, Amy S. Ishiguro, Michael Ronco, Glenn Walters
Items.Title: Automated optical acceptance testing for Argus Array commissioning
Items.Abstract: The Argus Array is transitioning from its prototype phase to the production of a 1,200-telescope system designed to monitor 8,000 square degrees of the night sky. To ensure the quality of this large-scale deployment and optimize for survey depth, the team has developed an automated acceptance testing system for the Optical Tube Assemblies (OTAs). This system is designed to be a multi-point-source artificial star projector paired with custom Python software to autonomously vet incoming OTAs. Key features include off-axis point generation for sensor tip-tilt corrections, collimation measurements using a Hartman mask, and throughput verification. Additionally, the system employs a dynamic mount to test each OTA under the specific gravity vectors it will experience in the final array, ensuring critical performance standards are met before commissioning.

Items.Authors: Eden A. McEwen, Jared R. Males, Elena Tonucci, Sebastiaan Y. Haffert, Olivier Guyon, Joseph D. Long, Logan Pearce, Laird M. Close, Warren B. Foster, Kyle Van Gorkom, Alex D. Hedglen, Parker T. Johnson, Maggie Y. Kautz, Jay K. Kueny, Jialin Li, Joshua Liberman, Miles Lucas, Jennifer Lumbres, Matthijs Mars, Tiffany Nguyen, Avalon L. McLeod, Lauren Schatz, Katie Twitchell
Items.Title: Beta Pic b in the blue: high contrast detections from 0.6–0.9µm with MagAO-X
Items.Abstract: Direct imaging of young, self-luminous planets provides key insights into atmospheric composition, chemistry, and ultimately formation histories. The beta Pic system is an invaluable laboratory for understanding planet formation with two exoplanets assumed to have formed simultaneously. Photometry in the optical (λ < 1 µm) is especially powerful at constraining Teff due to the rapid spectral drop-off at shorter wavelengths. The Magellan Extreme Adaptive Optics (MagAO-X) visible light extreme AO instrument on the 6.5m Magellan Clay telescope is uniquely capable of high contrast and small inner working angle from wavelengths 0.4-1.0µm. We present the recent visible observations of beta Pic b with MagAO-X and the technology development that has enabled them. We also discuss the characterization of beta Pic c in z’ using the PIAACMC.

Items.Authors: Francis Fortin, Jean-Luc Atteia, Alix Nouvel de la Flèche, Hervé Valentin, Olivier Boulade, David Corre, Damien Turpin, Aurélia Secroun, Stéphane Basa, François Dolon, Johan Floriot, Jean-François Leborgne, Alan Watson, William Lee
Items.Title: CAGIRE: capturing gamma-ray burst infrared emission
Items.Abstract: CAGIRE (CApturing Gamma-ray burst InfRared Emission) is a near-infrared imager that will be mounted on the 1.3m COLIBRI telescope in the San Pedro Martir Observatory. One of its main goals is to follow-up gamma-ray bursts (GRBs) seen by the SVOM satellite and provide J and H band lightcurves of the fading afterglows. The robotic telescope combined with the VHF link with the satellite will allow CAGIRE to arrive very early on target (1 min. after the burst alerts). This is an ideal setup to maximize the chances of catching far away events (z > 6), produced by the first generation of stars (pop III) and thus probe the very early universe. CAGIRE will be operational by the end of 2026 and for a duration of 10 years.

Items.Authors: Gabriel Tayama, Denis Brousseau, David Aikens, Sudharsan Kalidoss, Ram Mohan Telikicherla, Abhishek Patkar, Vikas Chandan, Sreekar Karnati, Xiaopeng Li, Ben Walleshauser, Catherine Croson, Zebadiah Miles, Zhiyong Wang, Greg Radighieri, Dhanushkodidurai Mariappan, Simon Thibault
Items.Title: Capillary-operated stable mesoporous optical system (COSMOS): design update for the Zenith-DARPA program
Items.Abstract: We report recent progress on the COSMOS tiltable liquid mirror, developed under the DARPA Zenith program by GE Vernova in collaboration with Université Laval and Savy Optics. This scalable, non-rotating liquid mirror system features a dual-layer configuration: a ferrofluid base for magnetic actuation and a silver nanoparticle monolayer for high reflectivity. Surface shape and optical quality are actively controlled through capillary/adhesion and magnetic body forces generated by three separate sets of electromagnetic coils operating in a closed-loop enviroment with a deflectometry-based wavefront sensor. In this work, we present the construction and performance of up to 18 cm diameter prototype. We demonstrated closed loop operation with tilting up to 1 degree and the ability to achieve a liquid surface with 1.7 meters radius of curvature.

Items.Authors: B. Neichel, T. Fusco, F. Oyarzun, V. Chamboulyeron, J.-F. Sauvage, C.-T. Héritier, J. Charton, C. Pravert, F. Clop, L. Maillet, M. Laslandes, J.-L. Gach, D. Boutolleau, P. Feautrier, P. Bruno, Y. Wanwanscappel, C. Brémond
Items.Title: Cassiopee: defining the next-generation deformable mirror and high-speed SWIR camera for adaptive optics applications
Items.Abstract: Future Adaptive Optics (AO) for astronomy, optical communications, space surveillance, and defense require ultra-fast, high-precision components. We introduce a systematic method to define performance specifications for two such technologies: a large-format, high-cadence SWIR camera and a high-order deformable mirror (DM).    Using representative use-cases—including exoplanet imaging, free-space optical links, and satellite tracking—we build AO error budgets that drive quantitative requirements for DM architecture and camera performance. These specifications guide the design of a dedicated laboratory testbed for full AO-loop validation.    Finally, we outline the roadmap toward on-sky tests with the EKARUS facility at Asiago Observatory, enabling end-to-end demonstration and paving the way for next-generation AO systems on large telescopes and optical links.

Items.Authors: Ronan Higgins, Stephen Parshley
Items.Title: CCAT: using a laser metrology system for mirror panel alignment
Items.Abstract: The Fred Young Submillimeter Telescope (FYST) is a 6-m telescope under construction by the CCAT consortium at 5600 m on Cerro Chajnantor. Designed for observations from 100 GHz to 1.5 THz, it targets a total wavefront error below 10.7 μm. Meeting the wavefront requirements depends on precise alignment of the mirrors and mirror panels. A laser metrology system will measure these alignments with 2 μm accuracy. The mirror enclosure rotates in elevation with the mirrors, panel alignment can be measured at all elevation angles—an advantage over techniques such as holography or photogrammetry. This real-time system enables characterization of gravity and thermal effects. We present the system design, system testing in Germany, and initial results from Chile.

Items.Authors: Olaf Dambon, Clemens Dicke, Jessica Nelson
Items.Title: Challenges in the fabrication of large aluminum mirrors by means of diamond turning
Items.Abstract: The fabrication of large aluminum mirrors for astronomical instrumentation involves significant optical, mechanical, and thermal challenges. Aluminum enables lightweight structures and efficient machining, yet achieving high‑precision surfaces through diamond turning becomes increasingly demanding with growing mirror size. This contribution outlines key factors influencing manufacturing quality, focusing on material behavior, thermal treatment, and stress‑relief processes that affect dimensional stability. Strategies for optimizing diamond‑turning parameters to meet stringent surface specifications are discussed, along with coating‑related constraints arising from substrate microstructure and residual stresses. Insights and results from recent projects highlight both limitations and opportunities for advancing aluminum mirror technology in modern astronomical systems.

Items.Authors: Hagyong Kihm, Ma. Angela Lourdes B. Lequiron
Items.Title: Characteristics of carbon deposition of ion beam figuring method
Items.Abstract: We present the characteristics of a carbon deposition layer formed on a mirror surface during the ion beam figuring (IBF) process. IBF is widely used for precision optics manufacturing due to its highly deterministic, non-contact advantages over conventional polishing methods. However, the sputtered carbon particles from the ion source aperture, which is typically made of pyrolytic graphite, can be deposited on the target surface during figuring. The additive carbon layer must be eliminated, and characterizing its thickness distribution and etch rate is crucial for post-processing. We propose a new footprint model and a dwell time path generation for an adaptive ion beam figuring method that minimizes carbon deposition.

Items.Authors: Nikoli Cooper, Ramya Anche, William Melby, Joanna Rosenbluth, Kyle Van Gorkom, Ewan Douglas
Items.Title: Characterization and coronagraphic performance of a dichroic mirror on a high-contrast imaging testbed
Items.Abstract: The Habitable Worlds Observatory (HWO) is designed to directly image habitable exoplanets with a high-contrast imaging instrument operating from the ultraviolet through the infrared. A dichroic mirror used to create separate wavelength channels may introduce polarization aberrations that degrade the contrast performance of the coronagraph. To quantify these effects, we measure the Mueller matrix of a Thorlabs dichroic using a dual rotating Mueller matrix polarimeter. The dichroic mirror is then installed on the Space Coronagraph Optical Bench (SCoOB) to estimate the contrast performance. In parallel, the Mueller matrix of the dichroic is modeled in Python using polarization raytracing and propagated through a coronagraph with High Contrast Imaging in Python to measure the polarization aberrations of the dichroic in the system. By comparing these two contrast performance measurements, we demonstrate the achievable performance of a high-contrast coronagraph with a dichroic mirror.

Items.Authors: Jehanne Sarrazin, Amira Bouikni, Elsa Huby, Sylvestre Lacour, Mathias Nowak, Jean-Tristan Buey, Manon Lallement, Senol Yazici, Zexuan Wu
Items.Title: Characterization of a J-band integrated circuit for PLANETES, an upgraded high-contrast interferometer for the VLTI
Items.Abstract: Photonic Integrated Circuits (PICs) are miniaturized optical systems for stable and compact light manipulation. In Astronomy, they are not yet well adapted for use over a broad range of wavelengths, especially when nearing the visible light. PLANETES proposes to face these challenges for high contrast exoplanet detection, and extend the capabilities of GRAVITY (VLTI) from the K-band to the J-band.  In this poster, I will report on the efforts to design and test a high performance PIC for the recombination of four input beams, including an input dedicated to the monitoring of the instrumental phase variations, a critical step to reach high contrast capabilities. I will present the photometric and interferometric results obtained with our first PIC prototype for PLANETES, characterized on our bench at the Paris Observatory

Items.Authors: Yukio Katsukawa, Yusuke Kawabata, Toshihiro Tsuzuki, Hirohisa Hara, Noriyuki Narukage, Toshifumi Shimizu, Hideki Kato, Luca Teriaca, Udo Schühle, Regina Aznar Cuadrado, Tobias Fiedler, Torsten Feigl, Benjamin Guiton, Shota Narasaki, Akihiro Fujie
Items.Title: Characterization of micro-roughness properties of the primary mirror in SOLAR-C EUVST
Items.Abstract: The EUV High Throughput Spectroscopic Telescope (EUVST) aboard SOLAR-C employs a 28 cm primary mirror with multi-layer coating for 17-122 nm wavelengths. The primary mirror must achieve high angular resolution with high sensitivity and minimal scattering at the shortest wavelength while withstanding 90 °C orbital temperatures, requiring Zerodur for its ultra-low thermal expansion. The required surface figure accuracy is achieved by ion beam figuring, but it may degrade small-scale surface roughness, requiring careful characterization. We used three-scale measurements: interferometry (>1 mm), white-light microscopic interferometry (1 µm to 0.5 mm), and atomic force microscopy (10 nm to 5 µm). These measurements yielded power spectral distributions, which we converted to point spread functions (PSFs) with scattering wings. Reflectivity measurements confirmed consistency with the PSFs. Scientific impact was evaluated by convolving the PSFs with simulated coronal images.

Items.Authors: Tanya Das, Andreas Seifahrt, Jacob L. Bean, Julian Stürmer, Ze'ev Vladimir, Nina Brown, Ritvik Basant
Items.Title: Characterizing fiber and detector systematics of the MAROON-X EPRV spectrograph on Gemini North
Items.Abstract: MAROON-X is an extreme precision, fiber-fed spectrograph on Gemini North, with a resolving power of 85,000 over 500-920 nm. It uses a Fabry-Pérot etalon for simultaneous wavelength calibration and a microlens-based pupil slicer to feed three science fibers that are later combined into a virtual fiber for radial velocity (RV) extraction. We investigate fiber related systematics affecting RV precision, focusing on how focal ratio degradation (FRD) and fiber scrambling influence measured velocities. Using transit data and observations of RV standards, we assess FRD stability, its sensitivity to instrument re-installation, and its impact on flux balance between fibers. We also perform scrambling tests with etalon calibration data to probe sensitivity to guiding and focus variations. Additionally, we characterize CCD charge transfer inefficiency (CTI) and its contribution to the overall RV error budget. These analysis help ensure the long-term stability and reliable performance of MAROON-X.

Items.Authors: Vincent Benz, Wolfgang Gaessler, Jake Pember, Andreas Quirrenbach, Christian Schwab, Julian Stuermer
Items.Title: Characterizing modal noise in high-resolution Echelle spectra using flat-field images
Items.Abstract: Modal noise remains a limiting factor in the stability of fiber-fed high-resolution spectrographs. In this proceeding, we describe a method to quantify spatial frequency modulations and temporal evolution of modal noise using spectral flat-field images. Analysis of the spectral orders reveals structural patterns, which exhibit clear time dependence and vary with fiber core size.  Fourier analysis shows known modal noise characteristics, such as noise being dominated by low spatial frequencies and worsening toward longer wavelengths. These effects are suppressed by agitation and grow in severity for a lower number of active modes. In a worst-case scenario for a static few-mode fiber, peak-to-valley noise levels reach 12% of the mean flux.

Items.Authors: Qiqige Xin, Jean Louis Lizon, Bin Yu, MingDa Jiang, DingHao Feng, Kai Zhang, Wei Xing, Francisco Javier Castro Lopez, Benjamin Siegel, German Prieto
Items.Title: CHORUS on GTC: a different opto-mechanical approach for CHORUS high resolution spectrograph
Items.Abstract: The Canary High Optical Resolution Ultra-stable Spectrograph (CHORUS) is a high resolution spectrographic facility for the GTC in La Palma. The facility includes an ultra stable spectrograph for radial velocity measurements: CHORUS VIS for Visible Band Spectrograph. If some important sub-systems like the detector cryostats and the echelle mosaic are direct heritage from ESPRESSO, the mechanical design departs from the one of the ESO VLT instrument. The paper documents how this design shall for example offer a longer vacuum autonomy without active pumping. The design of the optical bench as well as the implantation of the various optical components should also guaranty an easy and straight forward alignment.

Items.Authors: Jiajia Wu, Fujia Du, Qiqige Xin, Liang Tang, Jean-Louis Lizon, Kai Zhang
Items.Title: CHORUS on GTC: environment control system (ECS)
Items.Abstract: The Canary High Optical Resolution Ultra-stable Spectrograph (CHORUS) is a high resolution spectrographic facility for the GTC in La Palma. The facility includes high resolution spectrograph working in the visible band (VIS) and an ultraviolet spectrometer (UVS), The paper presents the Environmental Control System designed to ensure internal optical stability.

Items.Authors: Daniel Smith, Sebastiaan Y. Haffert, Siddharth Maharana, Matthias Tecza, Miles Lucas, Maud Langlois, Frans Snik
Items.Title: Closing the technology gap for the Extremely Large Telescope’s Planetary Camera and Spectrograph (ELT-PCS): Development of Polarimetric Imaging and Spectroscopy for Exoplanet Characterisation
Items.Abstract: The Planetary Camera and Spectrograph (PCS) will be the Extremely Large Telescope’s dedicated instrument for exoplanet characterisation, with a central goal of discovering and studying rocky exoplanets. We report on the development of the polarimetric imaging and spectroscopy activities within the ELT-PCS Science Instrumentation work package. Polarimetry provides a complementary detection channel by enhancing discrimination between residual stellar speckle noise and polarised signals originating from exoplanet atmospheres and circumstellar environments. Current efforts focus on identifying the key science and technical drivers for imaging polarimetry and spectro-polarimetry across visible and near-infrared wavelengths, including instrumental polarisation effects from the ELT optical train, calibration limitations, modulation strategies, polarisation-induced systematics, and the integration of integral field units (IFUs) for spatially resolved spectro-polarimetric observations.

Items.Authors: Sebastiaan Y. Haffert, Axel Potier, Lucie Leboulleux, Bachar Wehbe, Adam Taras, Anthony Boccaletti, Arthur Vigan, Carlos Correia, Caroline Kulcsár, Charles Sallard, Dimitri Mawet, Elena Tonucci, Elsa Huby, Fernando Pedichini, Gilles Orban de Xivry, Henri-François Raynaud, Iremsu Taskin, Iva Laginja, Jalo Nousiainen, Johan Mazoyer, Jonas Kühn, Julia Seidel, Louis Desdoigts, Lucas Marquis, Mamadou N'Diaye, Matthijs Mars, Maud Langlois, Nicolas Galland, Olivier Absil, Patrice Martinez, Pierre Baudoz, Raphaël Galicher, Raphael Poucelot, Rico Landman, Valentin Fonteneau, Vincent Chambouleyron, Yinzi Xin
Items.Title: Closing the technology gap for the Extremely Large Telescope’s Planetary Camera and Spectrograph (ELT-PCS): development of the coronagraph and focal plane wavefront control strategies
Items.Abstract: The Planetary Camera and Spectrograph (PCS) will be the ELT’s dedicated instrument for exoplanet characterization, with a central goal of discovering and studying rocky exoplanets. To prepare for these ambitious objectives, the PCS R&D consortium, launched in January 2025 under ESO’s leadership, was established to advance the conceptual design and bridge critical technology gaps. We will report on the progress of the coronagraph and focal-plane wavefront control work package. Our efforts focus on the development of coronagraphs tailored for PCS and on strategies for integrating wavefront control into their operation. A key component of this work is the PCS Coronagraph Evaluation Pipeline (PCS-CEP), designed to provide a uniform framework for assessing coronagraph performance and wavefront control, an approach inspired by the Habitable Worlds Observatory coronagraph design survey. PCS-CEP enables a fair comparison of diverse concepts, ensuring a level playing field for innovation.

Items.Authors: William A. Podgorski, Mark Mueller, Colby Jurgenson, Andrew Szentgyorgyi, Cem Onyuksel, Matthew Smith, Abigail Unger, Kenneth McCracken, Daniel Baldwin
Items.Title: Co-alignment of the GMT-Consortium Large Earth Finder (G-CLEF) spectrograph three segment Echelle grating
Items.Abstract: The G-CLEF R4 Echelle grating is a key optical component in the G-CLEF spectrograph. The Echelle grating disperses the light over the 350 nm to 900 nm wavelength range into 111 usable orders which are then cross-dispersed and imaged as echellograms in the two G-CLEF cameras. In order to achieve the required spectral resolution, the G-CLEF grating is 1260 x 320 mm in size. Since this exceeds the maximum size of the Richardson Grating Lab’s production capability, the G-CLEF grating is made from three 420 x 320 mm segments, which are the largest size that can be produced. In order to function as a single grating, the three segments must be co-aligned to arc-second tolerances and must maintain this alignment throughout assembly and operation. In this paper we discuss the novel mechanical adjustment and preloading methodology, which were implemented to rapidly align the grating segments, and the structure which supports the adjusters. We also discuss the alignment and measurement technique

Items.Authors: Célestin Libert, Tanguy Thibert, Pierre Guiton, Gary Lejeune, Emile Ruwet, Isabelle Tychon, Sylvie Liébecq, Juan-Felipe Simar, Jérôme Jacobs, Jean-Yves Plesseria
Items.Title: Comet interceptor scan mirror assembly: AIV of the qualification model
Items.Abstract: Comet Interceptor is a fast-class mission in ESA’s Cosmic Vision Program comprising three spacecrafts. With a short development process challenge, it will be the first mission to visit a Long Period Comet that is starting its journey in the inner Solar System. The Rotating Mirror Assembly is mounted on the Comet Interceptor spacecraft A, rotating a mirror facing the Comet Camera instrument. The rotation allows continuous observations during the flyby. It is composed of the Scan Mirror Assembly (SMA), the CSL’s contribution, and the Scan Mirror Electronics (SME) from Thales Alenia Space Switzerland. The SMA is constituted of mirror assembly with a baffle, a mirror, a dust shield, and a rotation mechanism below. In this paper, the design of the SMA is presented, and the main result of the integration, assembly and test campaign of the Qualification Model (QM) are discussed. A conclusion summarizes the actual status of the project and presents the next activities planned.

Items.Authors: Chris R. Benn, Lilian Domínguez, Marc Balcells, Cecilia Farina, Nada Ihanec, Nicholas Jannsen, Eduardo Mantero, Javier Mendez, Neil O'Mahony, Yeisson Osorio, Ruben Sanchez, Saskia Schlagenhauf, Lucia Suarez, Gavin Dalton
Items.Title: Commissioning of the WEAVE spectrograph on the William Herschel Telescope
Items.Abstract: A new wide-field multi-object spectrograph, WEAVE, built by an international consortium, has been installed at the prime focus of the 4.2-m William Herschel Telescope on La Palma. WEAVE allows up to 1000 objects (one per fibre, over a field of view of diameter 2 deg), to be observed simultaneously, with spectroscopic resolution R ~ 5000 or R ~  20000. WEAVE also has two integral-field modes, allowing observation of either 20 small fields with diameter 12 arcsec, or 1 large field with diameter 90 arcsec. WEAVE was designed to satisfy the need for large follow-up spectroscopic campaigns complementing surveys by major space (e.g. Gaia) and ground-based (e.g. LOFAR) facilities, and is expected to deliver ~ 10 million spectra over the next few years.    Here we report on the commissioning of the instrument, describe the challenges met along the way, and summarise the current state of the instrument.

Items.Authors: Pierce Morgan
Items.Title: Compact telescopes for proliferated space missions
Items.Abstract: The Monolithic Telescope technology, developed at LLNL and now being commercialized by Starris Space Systems of Optimax, offers an innovative optical architecture for compact, highly stable space payloads. Made from a single piece of fused silica with primary and secondary surfaces polished on opposite sides, the Monolith removes alignment structures while maintaining diffraction-limited performance. Compared to Cassegrain designs, it provides reduced length and mass, excellent optical quality, and strong resilience to vibration, shock, and thermal variation, enabling high-performance imaging on smaller spacecraft with lower SWaP. Several configurations have been space-qualified or flown, demonstrating maturity and manufacturability. This talk reviews the transition from LLNL research to producible systems, including design and manufacturing methods, test results, and efforts to extend the technology to new mission classes and optical configurations.

Items.Authors: Yu Zhou, Boqi Men, Liqian Xia, Xiaohang Zhang, Tommaso Ghigna, Suerfu Burkhant
Items.Title: Concept design of an ultrafast transition-edge sensor as the detector terminal of a Fourier-transform spectrometer for high-dynamic-range solar observations
Items.Abstract: Mid-infrared spectroscopy near 12 µm enables key diagnostics of the solar atmosphere, but requires detectors with high dynamic range, fast response, and low noise under strong photon loading. We present a concept for an ultrafast transition-edge sensor (TES) integrated into a Fourier-transform spectrometer for solar observations in the 12 µm band. The design targets a 50 µs response with photon-noise-limited performance and sub-µW saturation power using a niobium TES and low-heat-capacity tantalum absorber optimized for mid-IR coupling. Tuned thermal conductance and Tc enable rapid recovery from interferometric modulation. A cryogenic attenuation chain regulates solar loading. A cryogenic HEMT low-noise amplifier provides MHz-class bandwidth to capture high-contrast, rapidly scanned interferograms. This concept demonstrates a feasible path toward high-dynamic-range mid-IR TES devices for future high-cadence solar spectroscopy and imaging.

Items.Authors: Itsuki Sakon, Takeo Minezaki, Hiroaki Sameshima, Takashi Miyata, Yuzuru Yoshii, Takahiro Nagayama, Hidehiko Nakaya, Yuji Ikeda, Keiichi Maeda, Masaomi Tanaka, Nozomu Tominaga, Hideyuki Umeda, Buell T. Jannuzi, Peter A. Strittmatter, David J. Sand, Thomas W. Folkers
Items.Title: Conceptual design of the MAGNUM near-infrared four-band imager (MAGNIFI) for 2-m MAGNUM telescope
Items.Abstract: We present the results of conceptual designing of a near-infrared four-band simultaneous imaging instrument—the MAGNUM Near-Infrared Four-band Imager (MAGNIFI)—for installation on the 2-m MAGNUM telescope. The MAGNIFI aims to simultaneously capture the Y (1.032µm), J (1.235µm), H (1.162µm), and Ks (2.159µm) bands. Optical design studies have adopted an F-conversion optical system (F/9.19 to F/6), followed by an Offner relay and three beam splitters to divide light into four channels corresponding to the Y, J, H, and Ks bands, thus realizing simultaneous imaging across 0.9--2.3µm. All channels are planned employ InGaAs detectors manufactured by Hamamatsu Photonics, providing a wide field of view of 3.7 arcmin by 3.0 arcmin. MAGNIFI will enable multi-color, near-infrared imaging contributing to both time-domain and multi-messenger astronomy. In this presentation, we introduce the results of the conceptual design of MAGNIFI and outline the science cases the instrument aims to address.

Items.Authors: In-Ung Song, Chang-Jin Oh, Andrew E. Lowman, Jamison C. Noenickx, Sukmock Lee, Connie Rockosi, Tim Miller
Items.Title: Conceptual design of wavefront sensing for the Spec-S5 large wide field segmented telescope
Items.Abstract: This study employs dispersed fringe sensors (DFS) and a phase retrieval (PR) scheme to co-phase the primary mirror segments and assess system performance of the Spec-S5 telescope. DFS measures relative piston values between adjacent segments to align the eight primary mirror segments, while PR detects fine-scale wavefront errors using multiple image sensors positioned at the center and edges of the image plane. These sensors enable single-shot measurements through a custom octagonal wedged Grism and field diversity concept. Validation on a test bench with a commercial telescope confirmed performance better than 100 nm RMS, demonstrating the suitability of DFS and PR for Spec-S5.

Items.Authors: Silvia Regalado Olivares, María Jesús Martínez González, Patricia Gómez González, Carlos Quintero Noda, Jonai Bienes Pérez, Antonio Matta-Gómez
Items.Title: Conceptual optical design of EMBER, the infrared integral field spectropolarimeter for EST
Items.Abstract: EMBER is the infrared integral field spectropolarimeter for the European Solar Telescope (EST). The instrument is a high-resolution spectrograph that will cover the solar spectrum from 1 to 2.2 μm and is optimised for 1.083 μm. In addition, it will provide spectropolarimetric observations using a dual-beam configuration. The spectrograph follows a Czerny-Turner design and will observe a 2D input field of view (FoV) of 10” x 10”. This wide FoV will be reorganised by a slicer mirror-based Integral Field Unit (IFU) that is composed by 400 slicers. The IFU output is subsequently rearranged into 10 slits that feed the spectrograph. This work presents the current status of the conceptual optical design of EMBER.

Items.Authors: Peter Spanoudakis, Mathias Gumy, Yves-Julien Regamey, Cyril Rupf, Juan Lahera Perez, Jonathan Bennès, Philippe Schwab, Stéphane Humbert
Items.Title: Configurable slit unit development for the Magellan infrared multi-object spectrograph (MIRMOS)
Items.Abstract: The MIRMOS instrument will integrate a reconfigurable slit mask unit (CSU) which is a mechanism allowing to generate a multi-slit configuration at the focal plane of the telescope. The CSU creates slits on the focal plane by displacing two opposing bars with the space between them creating a slit and allowing light of a selected object to be transmitted to the detector. The mechanism is being developed for the Magellan InfraRed Multi-Object Spectrograph (MIRMOS) instrument to be installed on one of the two 6.5m Magellan telescopes at the Las Campanas Observatory in Chile. MIRMOS will provide NIR multi-object spectroscopy over a field of view of 3' x 13'. The reconfigurable mask allows the formation of 92 optical slits in a 66 x 266 mm2 field of view. The mechanism is a derivative design from the successful MOSFIRE CSU in operation on the Keck Observatory since 2012.

Items.Authors: Jared A. Termini, Keri Hoadley, Casey DeRoo, Cecilia R. Fasano, Fernando Cruz Aguirre, Paul Scowen, Manuel Quijada, Mateo Batkis, Luis Rodriguez de Marcos, Javier Del Hoyo, Gavin Frueh
Items.Title: Connecting the fabrication quality and UV performance of gratings to predict the UV performance of large-format gratings
Items.Abstract: UV spectroscopy is a powerful tool for probing astrophysical systems, as it traces baryonic matter across many phases and temperatures. Achieving our future science goals will require high-performance, large-format gratings, but directly measuring their UV efficiency is costly and time-consuming. If trends between the UV performance and fabrication quality of small gratings can predict the performance of larger gratings, we can streamline the UV grating characterization process.    We present results from a multi-year study assessing fabrication quality and UV performance of small gratings. We use optical interferometry to determine the gratings’ period error and limiting resolution. We use single-point metrology to measure the surface roughness. We characterize the gratings’ UV performance via efficiency measurements from 900-2000Å. We investigate correlations between fabrication metrics and UV performance, enabling metrology-based prediction of large-format grating performance.

Items.Authors: Ellen Schallig, Gavin Dalton, Ian Lewis, Scott Trager, Elfi Dijkstra, Emanuel Gafton, Menno de Haan, Rik ter Horst, Mike Irwin, Remko Stuik
Items.Title: Construction, integration and performance of the WEAVE LIFU
Items.Abstract: WEAVE is the new wide-field spectroscopy facility for the prime focus of the William Herschel Telescope in La Palma, Spain. It includes a large integral field unit (LIFU), which has a size of 90” x 78” on sky with a resolving power of up to R = 10,000. The array consists of 609 optical fibres; each fibre is 33 m long and has a core size of 170 µm. In this poster, we describe the details of the assembly process on both the input (sky) and the output (spectrograph) ends of the fibre bundle, and preliminary performance on sky.

Items.Authors: Mate Adamkovics
Items.Title: Coupling light into photonic circuit waveguides with micro-optics for scientific instrumentation
Items.Abstract: Instruments that incorporate integrated photonics can be designed to decrease size, improve stability, and implement novel functionality. Photonic technologies such as couplers/splitters, arrayed waveguide gratings, resonators, and modulators, can be used measure the information that is collected by telescopes in ways that are not possible with traditional optics. One specific application is the photonic coronagraph, which provides particularly high contrast using interferometric nulling. A critical challenge for using photonic devices in astronomical instruments is the coupling efficiently from free-space into the waveguides of the photonic integrated circuit (PIC). Grating couplers are one of the most common interfaces, yet they achieve a peak efficiency over a narrow spectral bandpass. We present our work on 3d-printed micro-optics for efficient wide-band coupling into PIC waveguides and discuss how efficient coupling into PICs can enable future space telescopes.

Items.Authors: Gerhard Ulbricht, Gary Donegan, Cáthal McAleer, Stephenie Brophy Lee, Lyra Quinlan, Mario De Lucia, Eoin Baldwin, Jack Piercy, Oisín Creaner, Piotr Wawer, Przemysław Nita, Deirdre Coffey, Tom Ray
Items.Title: Cryogenic qualification testing of the common optics dichroic filters 1 to 5 for ESA’s ARIEL mission
Items.Abstract: ARIEL, the Atmospheric Remote‐sensing Infrared Exoplanet Large‐survey mission, is ESA’s Cosmic Vision M4 mission and will study the atmospheres of up to 1000 exoplanets. It uses a set of five dichroic filters (D1 to D5) to split the incoming bandwidth of 0.5 to 7.8 μm and will operate between 40 K and 60 K. We will present ongoing efforts of qualification testing of the D1 - D5 dichroics. Our Tests are performed at ambient and cryogenic temperatures and include transmission and reflectivity spectra, the cryogenic shift of the dichroic’s transition wavelength, wave-front error measurements, humidity testing and cryogenic cycling between 37 K and 323 K. We will give a progress report and will elaborate on achieved results, experimental setups and encountered challenges. We will also discuss steps to establish an instrumentation clean room, suitable for flight acceptance testing for in-space instrumentation.

Items.Authors: Xianyi Zhou, Chuanxin Wei, Yonghe Chen, Jiaming Liang, Yanwu Kang, Yuji Zhu, Junfei Li
Items.Title: Cryogenic temperature compensation design for the optical structure of The Earth 2.0 (ET) Transit Telescope
Items.Abstract: This study addresses the thermal-structural matching challenge faced by the optical system of The Earth 2.0 (ET) Transit Telescope (comprising nine lenses with apertures of 276–344 mm) operating at –15 ℃. An optomechanical design integrating a two-stage flexible support structure with coefficient of thermal expansion (CTE)-matched materials is proposed, coupled with a low-temperature displacement pre-compensation method. By establishing a coupled thermal-structural-optical model, the predicted deformation is used as a feedforward correction in the alignment process to actively compensate for image quality drift under cryogenic conditions. The resulting system achieves an EE90 radius variation of less than 0.5 μm at –15 ℃, significantly enhancing on-orbit stability and providing a valuable reference for the development of similar cryogenic optical systems.

Items.Authors: Sibo Van Gool, Bart Vandenbussche, Gert Raskin, Hugues Sana, Leonardo Peri, Louis Storm, Julien Storm, Pierre Royer, Maddalena Reggiani, Matteo Mallia, Dirk Vandepitte, Dominic Bowman, Camille Pirat, Jan Goris
Items.Title: CubeSpec: development of the payload control unit for a high-resolution spectroscopy CubeSat
Items.Abstract: The CubeSpec mission at KU Leuven brings optical spectroscopy to a 12U CubeSat platform to study massive stars, addressing the challenge of integrating advanced instrumentation in a compact, power-limited spacecraft. High pointing stability is achieved through three piezo actuators rotating a Fine Steering Mirror in closed-loop feedback with a Fine Guidance Sensor and actuator strain-gauge readings. The guidance and science detectors use GSENSE2020BSI CMOS sensors, each interfaced by an Artix-7 FPGA and streamed to a Zynq-7000–based payload processor. Additional components include high-voltage piezo drivers, an ADXL355 microvibration experiment, and CSP-based links for onboard communication and science data transfer.

Items.Authors: Sydney Skorpen, Pradip Gatkine, Ian P. McLean, Jeremy Lin
Items.Title: Demonstration of an integrated R~30,000 astrophotonic spectrograph
Items.Abstract: By operating in the diffraction-limited regime, astrophotonic instruments break the scaling relationship between telescope and instrument sizes, unlocking increasingly high-resolution spectrographs in a compact, stable, and inexpensive format. Here, we present the results of integrating an R~30,000 chip-based arrayed waveguide grating (AWG) spectrograph sensitive to the NIR H-band (1.45-1.65 μm) in a packaged fiber-fed instrument, as well as on-sky testing. This assembly consists of the photonic spectrograph, followed by a cross-disperser to separate the spectral orders (each spanning ~12.5 nm waveband), and an InGaAs detector, all contained within a footprint equivalent to a shoebox. The package is made complete with a data-reduction pipeline that delivers wavelength-calibrated spectra. This pathfinder performance demonstration paves the way to mature facility-class photonic instruments, suitable for ground-based and space-based observatories.

Items.Authors: Dhwanil Patel, Sebastiaan Y. Haffert, Skyler Palatnick, Adam Taras, Maxwell Millar-Blanchaer, Matthjis Mars, Elena Tonucci, Jared R. Males, Laird M. Close, Joshua Liberman, Warren B. Foster, Kyle Van Gorkom, Olivier Guyon, Alexander D. Hedglen, Parker T. Johnson, Maggie Y. Kautz, Jay K. Kueny, Jialin Li, Joseph D. Long, Jennifer Lumbres, Eden A. McEwen, Avalon McLeod, Lauren Schatz, Katie Twitchell, Robert J. Harris, Viktoria Kutnohorsky
Items.Title: Demonstration of simultaneous PIAA-coronagraphy and wavefront sensing using a single metasurface-based focal-plane optic
Items.Abstract: Residual wavefront aberrations downstream of extreme adaptive optics systems produce quasi-static speckles that limit high-contrast imaging. To mitigate these non-common-path aberrations, highly sensitive focal-plane wavefront sensors such as Zernike wavefront sensors (ZWFSs) are used as second-stage correctors. Complex mask coronagraphs (CMCs) are also implemented in the focal plane. Both benefit from phase-induced amplitude apodization, motivating a combined focal-plane optic. Here, we demonstrate a hybrid metasurface designed to function as a ZWFS and a CMC in two intermediate-band H-band filters. Measurements of the fabricated metasurface show phase shifts of approximately π/2 at shorter wavelengths and π at longer wavelengths between 1.5–1.7 μm. On-sky tests with MagAO-X achieved a contrast of ~10⁻¹ at 1.6 μm, consistent with simulations based on metrology data. Finally, the dynamic range was evaluated using the MagAO-X internal source at 1.3 μm and compared with simulations.

Items.Authors: Jinyu Pan, Ru Chen, Haoran Yu, Lili Wang, Jun Li, Yi Chen, Hangxin Ji
Items.Title: Design and application of a balloon-borne ultraviolet spectrometer
Items.Abstract: This work reports a lightweight (＜10 kg) balloon-borne ultraviolet spectrometer engineered for continuous 200–400 nm measurements of key solar lines and atmospheric trace gases. Ground-based observations in this band are strongly attenuated, and current space missions lack full-band coverage. The instrument adopts a compact “slit–78 mm collimator–600 l/mm grating–105 mm imager–back-illuminated CMOS” layout, providing ~1.2 nm FWHM spectral resolution within a 450×370×160 mm envelope. Atmospheric transmission from 4–22 km was modeled using MODTRAN 6 and validated with Py6S, yielding a dedicated near-UV transmittance database to guide system design and performance assessment. The prototype has completed opto-mechanical integration, and wavelength and flux calibrations are ongoing. A ≥22 km, ≥4 h high-altitude balloon flight is scheduled to verify in-situ optical performance, detector sensitivity, and system stability, supporting future extended-altitude UV remote-sensing missions.

Items.Authors: Andrzej S. Piascik
Items.Title: Design and characterisation of LIRIC: offsetting a compact infrared sCMOS detector within the image-plane
Items.Abstract: We present the design and characterisation of the Liverpool InfraRed Imaging Camera (LIRIC) deployed on the 2.0m Liverpool Telescope on La Palma in 2025.  LIRIC employs a science grade sCMOS InGaAs detector with a usable imaging area of 607 x 510 pixels, providing a 3.0 x 2.5 arcmin field-of-view.  Wavelength is selectable with J (1.1-1.4 µm) or H (1.5-1.7µm) via an integral filter wheel, which also has a gold mirror for darks.  The compact and lightweight design of the camera assembly allows for rapid repositioning to 17 fixed offsets within the focal plane using a simple cam mechanism.  This provides an alternative to offsetting the telescope or a tip-tilt mirror for generating sky background images subtraction.

Items.Authors: Liurong Lin, Lucas Marquis, Ruben Tandon, Jonas G. Kühn
Items.Title: Design and implementation of a fast SLM-driven coherent differential imaging scheme for exoplanet high-contrast imaging
Items.Abstract: We present a fast SLM-based coherent differential imaging (CDI) framework designed to mitigate quasi-static and post-AO speckles that limit ground-based exoplanet imaging. Using synchronous zonal phase modulation in the focal-plane with an LCoS SLM, our approach distinguishes coherent speckles from astrophysical signals. Through simulations, we assess the impact of modulation parameters and astrophysical conditions on achievable contrast and inner working angle. With emerging low-noise high-speed NIR detectors, this time-domain CDI method may also address rapidly evolving post-AO residuals. We outline ongoing implementation efforts with a 400 Hz SLM paired with a C-RED One detector and describe plans for deployment as an upgrade to the PLACID instrument on the 4-m DAG telescope.

Items.Authors: Enrico Hilpert, Jan Kinast, Thomas Räthe, Eric Schmucker, Peter Bizenberger, Harald Baumeister, Conchi Cárdenas Vázquez, Thomas Peschel
Items.Title: Design and manufacturing of the METIS imager collimator system for ELT
Items.Abstract: The Metis Imager will be one of the first light instruments operating at Extremely Large Telescope. This talk will cover the design, simulation and manufacturing of the collimator system, one of three main optomechanical subsystems in the imager. Operating at a temperature of 40 K, the choice of materials is of crucial importance to retain mechanical and dimensional stability of the components. An all aluminum 6061 approach for metal mirrors and housing parts was selected to realize an athermal system. The presentation will give an overview of the manufacturing approach of the mirrors, including thermal stabilization, metrology and integration as well as the thermal and structural boundary conditions.

Items.Authors: Fernando Angeles, Luis A. Madrigal, Jorge Fuentes, Jaime Ruíz-Díaz-Soto, Leonardo Garcés, Alejandro Farah, Sebastian F. Sánchez
Items.Title: Design and optimization of a closed-loop liquid cooling system for an EMCCD camera operating under low illumination and extreme environmental conditions
Items.Abstract: This work presents the design and implementation of a critical subsystem for EBANO, a low-cost integral field spectrograph. While EBANO's main components are 3D-printed, its EMCCD camera requires extreme thermal stability for optimal performance. To address the significant heat generated by the detector's Peltier (TEC) system, the team developed a specialized liquid cooling system. The primary achievement of this system is its ability to maintain an exceptional temperature stability of 0.01 °C at the detector. The summary covers the thermal requirements, the mechanical design of the heat sink, and establishes this cooling system as essential for the success of the EBANO instrument.

Items.Authors: Shuangquan Chen, Qihang Zhang, Shuo Wang, Ping Zhang, Yonggang Gu, Chao Zhai
Items.Title: Design and optimization of the communication network for the new generation LAMOST fiber positioning system
Items.Abstract: To meet the urgent demand for 8,000 optical fiber positioning units of the new generation of LAMOST, this paper, based on the proposed double-layer CAN network architecture, completes the comprehensive upgrade and optimization of the communication network. The core work includes: upgrading the backbone of the entire network communication from the traditional CAN to CAN FD (covering the upper computer - intermediate node and intermediate node - child node), to solve the bandwidth bottleneck of large data volume; Redesign and optimize the communication hardware of the core hub center nodes in multiple versions; Establish an efficient and reliable three-level communication protocol. Experimental verification shows that the stability, throughput and real-time performance of the optimized communication network all meet the strict requirements of the system, providing key support for the efficient collaborative control of LAMOST's 8,000 optical fibers.

Items.Authors: Pierre Noiré, Matthieu Cuq, Anthony L'Hostis, Thierry Roux
Items.Title: Design and qualification of custom hexapod positioning systems for optical alignment in extreme environments
Items.Abstract: This paper presents the influence of environmental constraints on the engineering design of hexapod positioning systems. These six-degree-of-freedom devices are widely used in telescope alignment and Ground Support Equipment (GSE) for optical alignment and qualification. Designers must contend with a range of challenging conditions, including vacuum, cleanroom, low temperatures, radiation, outdoor exposure, seismic activity,…  We present recent developments in custom positioners, highlighting the manufacturer’s expertise in meeting stringent environmental and operational requirements. This overview aims to share the current state of the art in engineering practices for advanced positioning systems, with a focus on the technical challenges posed by demanding environmental conditions.

Items.Authors: Rafael Alves de Souza Ribeiro, Carlos Eduardo Fermino, Tommy Lazaneo Zirnberger, Decio de Moura Rinaldi, Tiago Giorgetti, Daiana Ribeiro Bortoletto, José Octavio Armani Paschoal, Cláudia Lúcia Mendes de Oliveira
Items.Title: Design and qualification of large-aperture optical shutters for astronomical instruments
Items.Abstract: The Prof. João Steiner Institute of Instrumentation and Data Science (Steiner Institute) has launched a program to develop and fabricate scientific-grade optical shutters. The initiative is intended to expand the availability of scientific-grade shutter systems for astronomical instrumentation, based on a formal technology transfer agreement between Bonn-Shutter GmbH i. L. and the Steiner Institute. Initial activities include revisiting product families, establishing mechanical and electronic design standards, updating qualification workflows for wide-aperture shutters used in imaging and spectroscopic instruments, and enhancing long-term service capabilities. This paper discusses the program’s motivation and initial technical progress, and outlines the role the Steiner Institute aims to play as a reliable, technically compatible source of shutter solutions for the astronomical community.

Items.Authors: Avi Patel, Kevin Bundy, Aditya Sengupta, Matthew DeMartino, Anna Gagnebin, Emiel Por, Majid Mohammad, Michael Arena, Aled Cuda, Kiana Ejercito, Stephen Eikenberry, Ben Mazin, Holger Schmidt
Items.Title: Design and simulation of a photonic lantern-inspired astrophotonic chip for spectral sensing
Items.Abstract: Compact astrophotonic sensors can trade general-purpose spectral coverage for task-specific wavelength discrimination in a small integrated footprint. Developed with the Mazin Lab at UC Santa Barbara, this chip couples a single-mode input into a multimode interference region and seven-port fanout, producing wavelength-dependent output power fingerprints for spectral retrieval. Using ANSYS Lumerical FDTD simulations in silicon nitride, we compare symmetric and staggered-release geometries and quantify throughput, wavelength-dependent changes in the seven-port output distribution, and sensitivity near a 745 nm design point. We optimize over the tested geometric parameter space and identify designs with improved throughput and wavelength discrimination, including increased throughput-weighted Fisher information relative to the baseline. These results suggest that lantern-inspired integrated photonics can enable compact, task-specific spectral sensors for astrophotonic applications.
